items.title: The quotient by the power-torsion submodule has no I-torsion, and power-torsion modules are closed under extensions
items.author: The Stacks Project Authors
items.work: Stacks Project, chapter more-algebra.tex (More on Algebra)
items.source_version: Stacks Project source tree, file more-algebra.tex, corpus local snapshot 20261012
items.difficulty_reason: The lemma takes a ring R and a finitely generated ideal I of R and asserts two things: that for any R-module M the quotient M/M[I^infinity] has no I-torsion, i.e. (M/M[I^infinity])[I] = 0; and that an extension of I-power torsion modules is again I-power torsion (source lines 24041-24048). The proof of the first statement is an explicit exponent computation. Given m in M whose image lies in (M/M[I^infinity])[I], one has I m contained in M[I^infinity]; writing I = (f_1, ..., f_t), this gives f_i m in M[I^infinity], so that I^{n_i} f_i m = 0 for some n_i > 0, and taking N = sum_i n_i + 2 yields I^N m = 0 (proof lines 24051-24055). Hence m maps to zero in M/M[I^infinity], which is the first statement (proof lines 24056-24057). The second statement is settled by a quotient argument: for a short exact sequence 0 -> M' -> M -> M'' -> 0 with M' and M'' both I-power torsion, one has M[I^infinity] containing M', so M/M[I^infinity] is a quotient of M'' and is therefore I-power torsion; combined with the first statement and the torsion-free criterion this forces it to be zero, so M is I-power torsion (proof lines 24060-24065). The non-routine content is the exponent bookkeeping in the first statement and the two-sided use of the first statement in the second.
